label: My disruptive internal state is ADHD-driven rather than anxiety-, sleep-, or mood-driven
summary: The load-bearing personal hypothesis. Three rival mechanisms confound it and none has been ruled out; it cannot advance until the internal state is described concretely.

label: My ASRS result places me on the ADHD trait continuum rather than in a yes/no category
summary: Framing rather than diagnosis: a Part A score at the cutoff situates me somewhere on a spectrum the literature treats dimensionally.

label: ADHD's latent structure is dimensional (a continuum), not a discrete taxon
summary: Taxometric analyses of ADHD symptom data repeatedly fail to recover a category boundary and instead fit a continuous latent dimension. Contested: some analyses recover categorical structure within clinical samples.

label: Clinical ADHD is the quantitative extreme of a continuously distributed, heritable trait
summary: Twin and molecular-genetic evidence that the same aetiological factors operate across the whole symptom range, so the diagnosis marks a position on a continuum rather than a distinct condition.

label: The DSM symptom-count threshold is an arbitrary cut on a continuum with no natural breakpoint
summary: Impairment and quality of life decline linearly across the trait range with no discontinuity, so any diagnostic cutoff is a clinical convention. Held live by the counter-argument that unbounded threshold-lowering risks overdiagnosis and net harm.

label: Major dimensional frameworks (RDoC, HiTOP, the p-factor) place ADHD within continuous, transdiagnostic spectra
summary: The leading post-DSM classification programmes are all dimensional and locate ADHD on graded spectra (externalizing/disinhibition, general psychopathology) rather than in a discrete box.

label: A positive ASRS screen warrants a full clinical evaluation
summary: The actionable claim. Holds regardless of how the ADHD-vs-mimics question resolves — the evaluation is what resolves it.

label: Higher ADHD-like traits are associated with weaker response inhibition
summary: Research-side claim, replicated by the Horváth study in a non-clinical sample and under dual-task load.

label: Rising ADHD-trait load progressively flattens the inhibition–learning trade-off
summary: The paper's core result: the compensatory learning advantage that normally accompanies weak inhibition breaks down at the high end of the trait continuum.

label: Inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity are distinct but strongly correlated, not orthogonal
summary: At the phenotype level the two DSM domains share a dominant general factor (latent r ≈ .68–.78); a bifactor structure fits best, so the domains are oblique rather than independent axes.

label: Rating-based and task-based measures of the same construct are only weakly related
summary: Questionnaire and performance measures of executive function correlate at about median r = .19 and assess different levels of cognition — so the two instrument families are near-orthogonal, not interchangeable.

label: ADHD arises through dissociable neurocognitive pathways, present in some individuals but not others
summary: Inhibitory, delay/reward and timing deficits are independent components whose co-occurrence is no greater than chance, and no single deficit is universal — the mechanism level is genuinely near-orthogonal.

label: No single instrument is diagnostic; valid assessment is multi-method across levels
summary: Ratings and tasks disagree, the best objective tasks are not decisive, and robust markers like reaction-time variability are not ADHD-specific — so discriminating ADHD (and its mimics) requires a multi-method evaluation, not one measure.

label: ADHD measures separate ADHD from healthy controls, but not from the mimics
summary: Ratings and tasks alike discriminate ADHD from typically developing controls, yet lose their edge against other clinical conditions — anxiety, mood, OCD — so no single instrument can rule out the differential. The measurement-side root of the ADHD-vs-anxiety tension.

label: Most adult-identified ADHD is late-identified rather than genuinely late-onset
summary: Birth cohorts found adult and childhood ADHD groups barely overlap, but careful repeated assessment excludes ~95% of screen-positive late-onset cases; survivors show childhood symptoms masked by cognitive strength. Compensation plus rising demand, not new onset.

label: The course of ADHD fluctuates rather than simply persisting or remitting
summary: Most of the MTA sample showed waxing and waning persistence and remission rather than stable persistence or recovery, making person-environment fit the appropriate frame — the temporal counterpart of the dimensional argument.

label: The ADHD sex ratio largely reflects referral and ascertainment, not underlying prevalence
summary: Clinic ratios far exceed community ratios in the same populations, high-symptom girls are diagnosed less often than high-symptom boys, and the gap narrows to ~1.5:1 in adulthood — the signature of under-detection rather than a true prevalence difference.

label: The arousal/state-regulation axis is shared with the mimics by construction, not by coincidence
summary: The cognitive-energetic model defines its energetic pools as responsive to stress, sleep-wake cycle and noise — so sleep debt and anxiety move the very variable ADHD is hypothesised to dysregulate. What may be ADHD-specific is the regulation, evidenced by condition-dependence.

label: Excessive mind-wandering is transdiagnostic rather than an ADHD marker
summary: Mind-wandering tracked anxiety independently of ADHD diagnosis and showed no categorical ADHD/non-ADHD difference, while correlating with inattention dimensionally — and it mediates ADHD symptoms' relationship to anxiety and depression.

label: Sleep debt is a strong rival for inattention but a weak one for internal restlessness
summary: Experimental sleep restriction reliably degrades attention and emotional lability in healthy people, but no experiment has shown it induces hyperactivity or impulsivity — narrowing which half of the picture sleep can explain.

label: Onset, trajectory and counterfactual — not symptom intensity — discriminate ADHD from anxiety
summary: Because both conditions produce internal restlessness and the rating items measuring it are partly anxiety items, the discriminating evidence is structural: whether the restlessness predates any anxiety, persists in its absence, is situational or constant, and whether its content is worry or topic-shifting.

label: The 'calm outside, churning inside' state is internalized hyperactivity — subjective restlessness — not overt motor hyperactivity
summary: DSM allows adult hyperactivity to present as subjective restlessness, and adults with ADHD report mental restlessness in place of fidgeting; the IRS measures it and separates ADHD from non-ADHD students. This reframes the internal state as the adult form of the hyperactive axis — but the same internalized presentation is where anxiety is hardest to distinguish from ADHD.

label: Cognitive disengagement (daydreamy, foggy, mentally slow) is a construct distinct from ADHD inattention and more tied to internalizing
summary: Factor-analytic and meta-analytic work separates cognitive disengagement syndrome (formerly SCT) from ADHD inattention and links it more to depression/internalizing than to hyperactivity/impulsivity. If the internal state is foggy and disengaged rather than restless, CDS — not ADHD hyperactivity — may be the better description, and it points toward the mood differential.

label: ADHD and anxiety co-occur far above chance across the lifespan
summary: Adult ADHD is highly comorbid with other DSM disorders, up to ~80% carry at least one, and ~25% of children with ADHD have an anxiety disorder. High comorbidity is why the ADHD-vs-anxiety differential is genuinely hard rather than a technicality — the two really do travel together.

label: Emotional dysregulation is a core feature of ADHD, not merely a comorbidity
summary: Emotion dysregulation is prevalent across the ADHD lifespan and a major contributor to impairment, and has been called a distinctive attribute of adult ADHD. But its status is explicitly unsettled: it is equally consistent with being a correlated-but-distinct dimension or a separate entity, so 'core' is one reading among three.

label: The DSM childhood-onset requirement is hard to verify from an adult's own recall, so collateral information matters
summary: DSM needs some symptoms present in childhood, but adult self-recall of childhood ADHD has a positive predictive value near 0.27, and young adults with ADHD tend to underreport. Guidelines therefore lean on contemporaneous records and collateral informants (a parent or partner). This bears directly on a first evaluation in adulthood with no childhood documentation.

label: A positive response to stimulant medication does not confirm ADHD
summary: Normal children given dextroamphetamine show the same reduced activity and improved cognition as hyperactive children, so there is no ADHD-specific or 'paradoxical' stimulant response. Improvement on a medication trial is therefore not diagnostic evidence — a treatment-response confound on the personal ADHD hypothesis.

label: Evidence-based treatments meaningfully reduce adult ADHD symptoms
summary: Medication (methylphenidate in youth, amphetamines in adults) has the largest short-term effects; CBT for adults reaches effect sizes comparable to well-established child behavioural treatments; mindfulness shows moderate but tentatively-framed benefit. Treatment works — separately from whether a given internal state is ADHD.

label: ADHD reflects altered function across large-scale brain networks, not a single region or lesion
summary: The older prefrontal-striatal model has given way to systems-level accounts spanning multiple resting-state networks (frontoparietal, dorsal attention, default, visual). There is no ADHD 'spot' in the brain; the biology is distributed and network-level, which is consistent with a graded, dimensional phenotype rather than a discrete lesion.

label: Structural brain differences in ADHD are real at the group level but too small to diagnose an individual
summary: The largest imaging studies (ENIGMA) find real but tiny group differences — subcortical volumes at Cohen's d around -0.1 to -0.2, cortical effects no larger, and no detectable cortical differences at all in adolescents or adults. Group-level signal does not license an individual scan-based diagnosis, and the adult null is especially relevant to a first evaluation in adulthood.

label: ADHD and autism co-occur far above chance
summary: Co-occurrence estimates run high (roughly 20–50% of children with ADHD meet ASD criteria and 30–80% of ASD children meet ADHD criteria). DSM-IV had barred diagnosing both, which suppressed research; DSM-5 now permits a dual diagnosis, and the overlap is now openly studied.

label: ADHD and autism share heritable and neurocognitive substrates
summary: Family and twin studies support partly shared familial-genetic origins, with candidate pleiotropic genes, and the two share impairments in social and executive functioning. The overlap is not merely superficial symptom sharing but reaches down to partly common causes.

label: Despite the overlap, ADHD and autism remain distinct diagnostic categories
summary: Shared genetics and impairments notwithstanding, the phenotypic presentations differ qualitatively and quantitatively enough that reviews conclude the two are sufficiently distinct to warrant separate diagnoses. Overlap at the level of causes does not collapse the clinical distinction.

label: ADHD and sleep problems are bidirectionally related, not a one-way mimic
summary: The sleep–ADHD relationship runs both ways and more: sleep loss degrades attention (the mimic direction), while ADHD is associated with markedly disturbed sleep, and the two may share causes. Treating sleep purely as a rival to rule out understates a genuinely multidirectional link.

label: Delayed circadian phase is highly prevalent in ADHD and may be intrinsic, not merely comorbid
summary: Delayed sleep phase and delayed melatonin onset appear in most adults with ADHD who have insomnia, and delayed sleep phase disorder is reported in 73–78% of people with ADHD. Some argue part of the symptomatology is a downstream consequence of chronic circadian delay — which would move sleep from mimic to component for a subgroup.

label: ADHD co-occurs with depression well above chance
summary: Depression is among the most frequent conditions accompanying ADHD, and people with an ADHD history carry a significantly elevated risk of major depression. The overlap is large enough that low mood and ADHD have to be considered together, not as alternatives.

label: ADHD is a developmental risk factor for later depression, plausibly causal
summary: Prospective data show ADHD in adolescence predicts later major depression after adjusting for confounders, and Mendelian-randomization evidence is consistent with a causal effect of ADHD genetic liability on major depression. This reframes some ADHD-plus-depression as ADHD giving rise to depression, not two independent conditions.

label: Under-identifying ADHD in girls and women is not benign — missed cases carry serious impairment, including elevated self-harm
summary: Longitudinal follow-up of childhood-diagnosed girls shows persistent impairment and markedly elevated suicide attempts and self-injury into early adulthood, and reviews single out self-harm as a heightened risk for females with ADHD. The under-recognition documented elsewhere therefore has real stakes, not merely epidemiological ones.

label: ADHD symptom expression in women fluctuates with reproductive hormones
summary: Within-person, ADHD symptoms in regularly-cycling women rise when estradiol falls relative to progesterone or testosterone, peaking in specific menstrual phases. Symptom severity can thus move with the hormonal cycle independently of the underlying trait — a female-specific source of variability that male-referenced criteria and single-timepoint assessments miss.

label: A leading theory casts ADHD as fundamentally a deficit in behavioral inhibition, from which other executive functions follow
summary: Barkley's unifying model makes behavioral inhibition the primary deficit and derives working memory, self-regulation of affect/motivation, internalized speech and reconstitution from it. Influential and organising, but the author cautions it needs far more testing — and the empirical record (see the necessary-nor-sufficient hypothesis) complicates a single-core-deficit reading.

label: Executive-function deficits are real and central in ADHD on average, but neither necessary nor sufficient
summary: Meta-analysis finds significant EF impairment across all domains (medium effect sizes, strongest for inhibition, vigilance, working memory, planning), yet the deficits are not universal among people with ADHD and not specific to it. EF weakness is one important component of a heterogeneous neuropsychology, not the defining lesion — consistent with the multiple-pathways view.

label: 'Rejection sensitive dysphoria' is a popular but under-validated label for a real, established phenomenon
summary: RSD spread through social media and clinical anecdote (coined by Dodson) rather than through validation studies, and critical appraisal flags limited empirical evidence plus risks of stigma and reifying it as innate. The experience it names is real and better captured by the established rejection-sensitivity construct — so the phenomenon is genuine even though the specific ADHD-syndrome label is not well grounded.

label: Heightened rejection sensitivity is an under-explored facet of ADHD-related emotional dysregulation
summary: Rejection sensitivity is treated as one aspect of the emotional dysregulation that is prevalent and impairing in ADHD, but the ADHD-specific evidence is thin — small, mostly qualitative studies. Plausible and clinically resonant, not yet firmly established, and not specific to ADHD (rejection sensitivity also marks depression, anxiety and personality disorders).

label: Hyperfocus is more prevalent in ADHD and may be a separable feature of the syndrome
summary: On new self-report measures, hyperfocus rises with ADHD symptomology and is higher in adult ADHD than controls, independent of stimulant use, prompting proposals that it is a separable dimension of ADHD. The evidence is young — new questionnaires, small-to-moderate samples — and hyperfocus is inconsistently defined and not specific to ADHD, so the claim is emerging rather than settled.

label: ADHD is better understood as dysregulated attention allocation than as a simple deficit of attention
summary: That the same people who cannot sustain attention on demand can also become unable to disengage from an absorbing task points to a regulation problem — attention deployed in the wrong amounts at the wrong times — rather than a straightforward shortage of attention. Hyperfocus is the over-deployed pole of that dysregulation.

label: ADHD is associated with consistent deficits in perceiving and reproducing time
summary: Reviews find ADHD consistently impaired across timing domains — motor timing, perceptual timing (duration discrimination and reproduction) and temporal foresight — from milliseconds to long intervals, alongside the lived sense that time slips away. Robust as a group-level finding; the felt 'time blindness' has a real cognitive basis.

label: Impaired time perception has been proposed as a possible diagnostic characteristic of ADHD
summary: Some reviews propose time-perception impairment as a candidate diagnostic feature of ADHD. But timing deficits are not specific to ADHD (they occur in other conditions), the measures and paradigms are heterogeneous, and the evidence needs replication — so the marker claim is a proposal, not an established diagnostic test.

label: Beyond attention and impulsivity, ADHD involves a motivation/reward-processing difference tied to the dopamine reward pathway
summary: There is increasing evidence of motivation deficits in ADHD, with PET data linking lower trait motivation to reduced dopamine reward-pathway function, and reviews casting an aberrant sensitivity to reinforcement as a core deficit. Motivation is a third axis alongside inattention and hyperactivity/impulsivity, not just willpower.

label: ADHD performance is strongly modulated by reinforcement, so it reflects reward-dependent regulation rather than fixed incapacity
summary: Reinforcement contingencies improve task performance and motivation in ADHD (somewhat more than in controls), and immediate reward is preferred to delayed. Being able to perform well when a task is interesting, urgent or rewarded — and poorly when it is not — is a reward-processing signature, not laziness or a stable inability.

label: Working-memory deficits are large, robust, central to ADHD models, and persist into adulthood
summary: Meta-analyses find working memory a prominent candidate primary deficit/endophenotype in ADHD, with large between-group effects (larger for spatial than verbal), independent of comorbidity and IQ, and persisting from childhood into adulthood. One of the most consistently replicated cognitive findings in ADHD — though, like other executive measures, not on its own diagnostic.

label: Excess movement in ADHD may be partly compensatory — aiding working memory rather than only impairing
summary: When gross motor activity was measured during working-memory tasks, higher activity predicted better working-memory performance in children with ADHD (but worse in typically developing children). This reframes at least some hyperactivity and restlessness as a compensatory mechanism recruited to support cognition, not purely a symptom to suppress.

label: Atypical sensory sensitivity (hyper- and hypo-) is elevated in ADHD and tracks ADHD traits dimensionally
summary: Adults and children with ADHD report more sensory hyper- and hyposensitivity than norm groups, and in the general population sensory difficulty rises with ADHD-trait level (a dose-response, all-modalities relationship). Consistent across clinical and non-clinical samples, fitting the trait-continuum view.

label: Sensory difficulties may be part of the ADHD phenotype itself, not merely autism comorbidity
summary: Sensory atypicality is a core feature of autism, and ADHD and autism co-occur — but atypical sensory profiles appear in adult ADHD irrespective of autistic symptoms, and general-population data suggest sensory difficulty could be part of the ADHD phenotype. The area remains under-studied and questionnaire-based, so this is emerging rather than settled.

label: In ADHD, comorbidity is the rule rather than the exception
summary: Most adults with ADHD carry at least one co-occurring psychiatric disorder — anxiety, mood, substance use, personality, autism, sleep and learning disorders foremost. This makes the differential usually a matter of 'and', not 'or': the question is rarely ADHD versus one rival but which conditions co-occur and how they interact.

label: ADHD elevates risk for substance use disorders, and is over-represented among people with SUD
summary: Prospective follow-up shows childhood ADHD predicts later abuse/dependence across nicotine, alcohol, marijuana and cocaine, and about a quarter of substance-use-disorder patients meet criteria for ADHD. The relationship runs both ways, making substance use a comorbidity worth screening for on either side.

label: ADHD is associated with lower self-esteem across the lifespan, built from accumulated negative feedback
summary: Children, adolescents and adults with ADHD score lower on self-esteem than controls, across domains and over long-term follow-up. The leading account is not that ADHD directly lowers self-worth but that growing up with negative messages, criticism and repeated underperformance erodes it — a consequence, not a core symptom.

label: Low self-esteem in ADHD is not fixed — it improves with treatment and support
summary: Self-esteem difficulties in ADHD respond to intervention: long-term outcome reviews find treatment associated with improvement in most self-esteem outcomes, and psychotherapeutic work can at least partly remedy them. The negative self-concept is a modifiable consequence, which matters for how the whole picture is framed.

label: ADHD is associated with poorer couple and family relationship quality, including higher divorce risk
summary: Adults with ADHD report poorer marital adjustment and family functioning, ADHD symptom levels predict lower romantic relationship quality, and parents raising a child with ADHD divorce more and sooner. The strain runs through both the couple (an adult partner's ADHD) and the family (parenting an ADHD child).

label: The relationship impact of ADHD is partly mediated by emotional dysregulation and conflict
summary: The link between ADHD symptoms and lower relationship quality is not direct: emotion-regulation problems and hostile conflict carry much of it. This ties relationship difficulty back to the emotional-dysregulation axis rather than to inattention alone, and points to what treatment might target.

label: The observable couple-conflict signature of ADHD is concentrated in the combined presentation, not inattentive-only
summary: When couples' conflict behaviour is coded directly, combined-type ADHD couples show more negativity and less positivity — tracking lower satisfaction — while inattentive-type couples look much like non-diagnosed couples. This locates the visible relational damage in the hyperactive-impulsive/combined phenotype and complicates a simple 'inattention strains relationships' account, though it rests on a single observational study.

label: Sexual dysfunction is markedly more prevalent in adults with ADHD than in the general population
summary: In a clinical ADHD sample, roughly four in ten adults screened positive for a sexual dysfunction — far above general-population rates — and such problems were almost never previously diagnosed. An under-recognised strand of intimacy and relationship difficulty, and an argument for screening sexual functioning during ADHD assessment. Rests so far on one clinic sample against population norms.

label: Physical (especially aerobic) exercise improves ADHD symptoms and executive function, acutely and chronically
summary: Meta-analyses and reviews find aerobic/cardio exercise produces moderate improvements in core ADHD symptoms (attention, hyperactivity, impulsivity) and in executive functions, with both acute post-bout effects and chronic effects of sustained training. A genuine, replicated behavioural benefit — plausibly catecholaminergic, in the same direction as medication.

label: The exercise benefit for ADHD is modest and dose-dependent — an adjunct, not a replacement
summary: Pooled effects on functional outcomes are modest (around g=0.6) and grow with longer intervention duration rather than intensity, so exercise complements rather than substitutes for other treatment. Real and worth doing, but not a stand-alone fix, and mostly studied in children.

label: The popular belief that sugar causes hyperactivity is not supported
summary: Blinded, placebo-controlled sugar-challenge studies find no effect of sugar on children's behaviour or cognition; the widespread parental conviction is attributed to expectancy and coincidental association. One of the most entrenched ADHD folk beliefs, and a false one.

label: Dietary interventions have small, variable effects on ADHD — helpful for some, not a primary treatment
summary: Restriction/elimination diets, food-color avoidance and omega-3 supplementation all show small effect sizes that benefit subgroups rather than everyone, with food-color effects especially bias-prone. Reasonable low-risk adjuncts with modest expectations, not a substitute for evaluation and standard treatment.

label: The association between screen/media use and ADHD-related behaviors is statistically small
summary: Across a meta-analysis (r+ = .12), a four-decade review, and a prospective cohort, screen media use is only weakly related to ADHD-related behaviors. The link is real but modest — far from the strong causal story of public worry.

label: Whether screen use causes ADHD is unresolved, and the relationship is plausibly bidirectional
summary: Even the prospective evidence stops short of causation, and reviews call explicitly for causal research. Reverse causation is plausible: ADHD-related reward-seeking and need for stimulation may drive intense screen use as much as the reverse, so screens may be an expression of the trait as well as a possible contributor.

label: Procrastination is strongly linked to ADHD — clinically central though not a formal criterion — driven especially by inattention
summary: Procrastination is routinely targeted in ADHD psychotherapy but is not an official DSM symptom; where studied, it correlates with ADHD-related behaviour, and specifically with inattention rather than impulsivity once the two are separated. A near-universal ADHD complaint that the diagnostic criteria do not name.

label: Procrastination is a self-regulation and delay-discounting failure, not a time-management flaw
summary: Procrastination is best understood as failure of self-regulation and volition — predicted by executive-function weaknesses and by impulsiveness, distractibility and task-delay, and captured by temporal-motivation/hyperbolic-discounting models. That profile is precisely ADHD's, so ADHD is the extreme of the procrastination-prone temperament rather than a separate story.

label: ADHD carries substantial stigma across the lifespan, driven largely by public doubt about the disorder’s validity
summary: People with ADHD symptoms of all ages face substantial stigma, prejudice and discrimination, and the most frequent stereotype is doubt about whether ADHD is a real disorder. The stigma rests substantially on a factual question the dimensional, genetic and neurobiological evidence in this notebook already answers.

label: Internalized stigma and anticipated discrimination are prevalent in adults with ADHD and add to the burden of disease
summary: A large fraction of adults with ADHD internalize stigma and anticipate discrimination, and these correlate with symptoms, distress, lower self-esteem, impairment and reduced quality of life. Stigma is not just an external attitude but a measurable added load carried by the person.

label: Improving sleep (behavioural sleep intervention / sleep hygiene) reduces ADHD symptoms, not just sleep problems
summary: A brief behavioural sleep intervention in children with ADHD reduced ADHD symptom severity and sleep problems, with part of the symptom benefit mediated through improved sleep; guidelines make healthy sleep practices the first-line response to sleep problems. Sleep is thus a genuinely modifiable lever on daytime symptoms, not only a comorbidity.

label: Melatonin reliably advances sleep onset and circadian phase in ADHD but does not directly improve ADHD symptoms
summary: In a randomised trial, melatonin advanced sleep onset and dim-light melatonin onset and increased total sleep, but had no significant effect on behaviour, cognition or quality of life. It targets the delayed body clock, which matters given the circadian delay common in ADHD, but is a sleep treatment rather than an ADHD treatment.

label: CBT-taught coping and self-management skills reduce ADHD symptoms, even in medicated adults
summary: A skills-based CBT (organisation, planning, coping, cognitive restructuring) added to stable medication lowered clinician- and self-rated ADHD symptoms and global severity relative to medication alone. Learnable coping strategies are an evidence-based lever that adds to, rather than merely substitutes for, other treatment.

label: Compensatory coping in ADHD works but is effortful, and its long-term quality-of-life payoff is uneven
summary: Adults with ADHD lean on effortful strategies — routine and habit, reframing, symptom-specific tactics — and simply must work harder than peers to keep up; yet the long-term quality-of-life benefit of coping-focused CBT was not confirmed. Coping reduces symptoms more reliably than it lifts life quality, and the effort itself is a cost worth naming.

label: Sex-hormone fluctuations modulate ADHD symptoms and cognition across the female lifespan
summary: Estrogen and related steroids regulate the neurotransmitter and signalling systems implicated in ADHD, so symptom expression can shift with the menstrual cycle and, by extension, across puberty, pregnancy/postpartum and perimenopause. A female-specific source of variability that male-referenced models and single-timepoint assessment miss.

label: Hormone-related mood conditions (PMDD, postpartum depression, climacteric symptoms) are more prevalent in women with ADHD
summary: Across reproductive transitions, women with ADHD report premenstrual dysphoric disorder and postpartum depression symptoms more often than the general population, plus elevated climacteric mood and somatic complaints. The hormonal sensitivity of ADHD shows up not just as symptom fluctuation but as raised risk of hormone-linked mood disorders.

label: The ADHD-creativity link is real but nuanced: a divergent-thinking advantage at trait level, for idea generation, not the clinical disorder or convergent thinking
summary: Increased divergent thinking (idea generation) is found mainly for high ADHD traits (subclinical) rather than the clinical disorder, with no advantage in convergent thinking (refining to one right answer), and stimulants do not overall reduce creativity. So the popular 'ADHD = creativity' claim is partly true but specific — a trait-level, idea-generation effect, not a superpower conferred by the disorder.

label: Real-world creative achievement is elevated in ADHD and driven by goal-directed motivation in self-selected domains
summary: Creative abilities and achievements are high in ADHD, and experimental work links this to goal-directed motivation (more original ideas when competing for a reward) and to selectively engaging domains that fit one's skills and interests. Creativity flourishes where interest and reward align — the reward-motivation account applied to a strength rather than a deficit.

label: Impulsivity in ADHD is not one thing but several dissociable facets with different biological bases
summary: Impulsivity fractionates into distinct components — motor/response inhibition (stop-signal), choice impulsivity (delay discounting), and emotional urgency — measured by different paradigms and with different neural substrates, and it sits within a broader self-regulation spanning action, emotion and cognition. A person can show one facet strongly and another not at all, consistent with the dissociable-pathways view.

label: Impulsivity is transdiagnostic — it describes ADHD but does not distinguish it
summary: Impulsivity is a component of many conditions (ADHD, mania, substance use), and stop-signal inhibition deficits appear in ADHD, OCD and schizophrenia at comparable magnitude. So 'impulsive' is a real feature of ADHD but a shared one — it characterises without discriminating.

label: ADHD's clinical heterogeneity has brain-derived structure: data-driven imaging clusters yield ~3 biotypes that roughly track the DSM presentations
summary: Clustering structural-MRI deviations without symptom input produced three ADHD biotypes (severe-combined with emotional dysregulation, hyperactive/impulsive, inattentive) that converge with DSM presentations, and an independent cortical-thickness study also found three subtypes — though different ones. Group-level evidence that the heterogeneity is biological, not a diagnostic scheme.

label: ADHD biotypes are likely salient regions along dimensional continua, not qualitatively distinct kinds
summary: The biotype study's own authors caution that their clusters may be points along underlying continua rather than distinct diagnostic entities, and cluster agreement was modest — consistent with ADHD as a graded trait where 'three types' is a convenient cut rather than three diseases.

label: Imaging biotypes cannot yet classify an individual or guide treatment
summary: Biotype findings are group-level, child-only, partly replicated, with case-control overlap; the neurochemical associations are exploratory spatial correlations that the authors say cannot inform treatment. A retrospective stimulant-response difference in a separate cortical-thickness study is a signal, not a prospective test. No scan assigns a person a type.
